Headline: "Andy Burnham to scrap digital ID to focus on 'helping with cost of living'"

Andy Burnham will scrap plans for a government-issued digital ID for all British adults when he becomes prime minister on Monday.
The move, which follows plans for new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, will shift focus to "the daily priorities facing people across the country", Burnham's office said.
Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government had already watered down proposals. In January, after nearly three million people signed a parliamentary petition opposing digital IDs, the government changed its approach; Cabinet Office minister Darren Jones unveiled a voluntary scheme.
Burnham's spokesperson: "time and resource that was going to be spent on a national ID scheme will go instead to where it's most needed, such as helping with the cost of living."
"One of the first things this government will do is put its focus where people need it right now" — scrapping digital ID will mean "redirecting the resources earmarked for the scheme towards people's everyday priorities".

Reaction — shadow technology secretary Julia Lopez (Conservative): accused Burnham of "trying to pretend he's riding to the rescue" after Labour "wasted millions of pounds on this project". "After pressure from the Conservatives, mandatory ID was already apparently off the table. Andy Burnham now needs to explain whether that was untrue, or whether he is simply claiming credit for a decision that had already been taken."

Kemi Badenoch (Conservative leader), interview on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg (BBC): warned Burnham's plans for government are "airy fairy"; accused him of not being aware of "what the country's priorities are"; said the country needs a leader ready to "take tough decisions"; described him as "a people pleaser".
